rows.en: Another kind of vow was the Naziriteship. This too appears to us in this ancient time in a wondrous light. According to the statute of the Torah, the Nazirite vows a vow with his mouth to separate himself as a Nazirite to the Lord (Numbers 6). Yet we are told that Samson, who judged Israel twenty years, was a Nazirite by the word of an angel who appeared to his mother and said to her: "Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and no razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb" (Judges 13). It is true that this Naziriteship is unique of its kind, for according to the narrative it came about by the word of the Lord (Nazir 4b); and we do not wish to draw conclusions from miraculous events, for in such things lies the boundary of the judgment of reason, and with them the domain of faith begins. But one thing we can draw from what is described in this story, namely, that in ancient times they made it a custom to dedicate a newborn child as a Nazirite to the Lord. We find a parallel to it in Samuel, who was likewise consecrated from the womb to be a Nazirite. This was not by a special command from the mouth of the Lord; only his mother consecrated him of her own free will, and he was a Nazirite all the days of his life (Nazir 66a). And although it is not stated explicitly that Samuel was a Nazirite, yet since there was put in his mother's mouth "and no razor shall come upon his head" [1 Samuel 1:11], we understand the intent of her other words, which she said, "and I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life" [1 Samuel 1:11]: that the meaning is the Naziriteship, for letting the hair of the head grow long is the sign of the Naziriteship. Now both of them, Samson and Samuel alike, defiled themselves with the dead (Judges 15:15;⚠1 1 Samuel 15:33), and they could not guard themselves from impurity although they were Nazirites all the days of their lives (Nazir 4b). Further, Samuel was a Nazirite by his mother's vow, and without doubt there were other such Nazirites in ancient times. This is also proved from the saying "for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb": thus the notion "a Nazirite to God from the womb" was not new, but was known and current in their mouths. And now we have seen that there is a kind of Naziriteship that a person does not take upon himself, and that even a woman may vow her son as a Nazirite (see Nazir 28b), and that there is a Naziriteship in which they did not guard themselves from impurity; and of all this there is nothing explicit in the statute of the written Torah before us. Here we see old traditions and understandings of the Torah, some of which agree with, and some of which differ from, the traditions that were handed down in the Oral Torah.

1.note: Print unclear (OCR מ"ט); read ט"ו, i.e. Judges 15:15, Samson and the jawbone.

rows.en: Around the days of the judgeship of the judge Ibzan — and in the opinion of some, Ibzan is Boaz — took place the event told to us of the history of Ruth the Moabite. According to what emerges from the scroll that tells this event, it appears that Israel in those days walked after its God, and the Israelite moral virtues stood in strength and might. This scroll presents to us a lovely picture of purity of virtues, of wholeness of hearts and of fitness in deeds of charity, which were widespread in that generation. From it we learn that there was at that time quiet and peace in the land, and proper order and arrangement in political affairs. This being so, we may firmly hold that whatever traces of the Torah are mentioned in this scroll did not turn to dross, and there is no admixture of foreign opinions in it; therefore it will be of great use for our purpose.{v1_02_15:1} It is told there that Ruth the Moabite, who returned with Naomi her mother-in-law from the field of Moab to the land of Judah, went down — on her mother-in-law's advice — to the threshing floor, to Boaz, who was a kinsman of the family of her dead husband, and asked him to spread his skirt over her, for he was a redeemer. Boaz consented to her request and said, "All that you say I will do" [Ruth 3:11], but since there is a redeemer nearer than I, I cannot redeem. And when the redeemer refused to redeem, then Boaz redeemed; and together with the redemption by which he redeemed the inheritance of the dead man, he also acquired Ruth the Moabite as his wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that his name be not cut off from Israel. If we consider this story, we find that Ruth's request was founded on nothing but the duty of levirate marriage. For so she said: "Spread therefore your skirt over your handmaid, for you are a redeemer" [Ruth 3:9]; that is, since he was a redeemer, it was for this reason his duty to spread his skirt over her and take her to himself as a wife. And this also emerges explicitly from the words of Boaz, who said: "Moreover Ruth the Moabite have I acquired to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren" [Ruth 4:10]. Close to these are the words said in the Torah in the law of levirate marriage, where a reason is given for this law: to raise up the name of the dead, so that the name of the dead be not blotted out of Israel [Deuteronomy 25:6–7]. Now there is no doubt that in the acquisition of Ruth, whom Boaz acquired as his wife, we have before us a description of the commandment of levirate marriage, which was a statute in Israel. But how was this commandment understood in its reason and in its purpose? This too becomes clear from the words of the scroll. There we see that this statute was brought in connection with the law of redemption, which was also a statute: that the nearest kinsman should redeem the inheritance of his kinsman. Therefore the law of levirate marriage was extended to all the kinsmen of the dead man, so that even if the dead man had no brothers, his widow would be taken in levirate marriage by one of his other kinsmen. Necessarily, then, the statute that speaks of the brother was not understood strictly, but as speaking of the usual case. Nor can we refute this understanding from the plain sense of the words of the statute. On the contrary, if we understand the end of the words of the statute, we may judge that there is no need to insist on the brother. For there a further saying is added: "the wife of the dead shall not be married abroad to a stranger" [Deuteronomy 25:5]; and this proves that the Torah warned only that the wife of the dead not be married to a stranger who is not of her dead husband's family; but in truth the nearest kinsman redeems, and he too raises up the name of the dead; and that the brother is mentioned is because he is the head and the first in the chain of kinship. And from this too we will not turn our eyes: it is clear that Ruth was bound in the bond of marriage while she was still a Moabite, and in the days of her widowhood she entered the religion of Israel. From this it appears that at that time a marriage bond between an Israelite man and a woman who was not of the daughters of Israel was valid. For if it had not been valid in their opinion, there would be no duty of levirate marriage upon the levir either. Necessarily such a marriage, once it had actually been carried out, counted with them as a marriage contracted according to religion. This scroll has further preserved for us one of the modes of acquisition in ancient times, called the drawing off of the shoe. For so it is told: "Now this was the custom in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning exchanging, to confirm all things: a man drew off his shoe and gave it to his neighbour" [Ruth 4:7]. It appears from this that in the days of the writer of the scroll the matter had already sunk into oblivion, and they no longer did so.{v1_02_16:1} Now from these particulars too we have learned that the laws of the Torah were carried out in different ways and were also understood in different ways, sometimes in agreement and sometimes in contradiction with their understanding in the Oral Torah; but however it may be, we have seen in this clear traces of traditions and interpretations concerning the statutes of the Torah.

But this time, the time of the nation's childhood, was like a cloudy morning. The sun of religion hid itself, and only at rare times did it come out for moments from the thickness of the cloud. Then, in the last period of the time of the Judges, suddenly, all at once, the clouds burst open and a new light spreads its wings over the full breadth of the land of Israel. A man in whom is the spirit of God, mighty in wisdom, glorious in understanding, and lofty and very high in moral teaching, he grew up as a tender plant out of a dry ground [Isaiah 53:2] and became a wonder among his people. From the womb and from birth God consecrated him and made him a prophet in Israel. And the man was — Samuel the seer. It was a time of stumbling for Jacob, and no spirit was left any longer in the deeds they did to fulfil the statutes and teachings of God; and their service of the Lord was a commandment of men learned by rote [Isaiah 29:13]. In the midst of this time Samuel arose and opened the springs of the Torah, which had been stopped up, at times by folly, at times by greed,⚠1 and at times by the weakness of the heads of the people and its leaders. The word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision (1 Samuel 3:1). The priests were the leaders of the people and led them astray, for they too did not walk uprightly. Moral teaching was despised; their heart was set on gain, and they did not know the Lord. Even when the people served the Lord, they did not serve Him alone, but set their heart on other gods as well (1 Samuel 7:3), and their faith turned to dross and their fear of the Lord became corrupt. To straighten such crooked things was the charge of Samuel; and his wisdom, the strength of his spirit, and the spirit of the Lord that stirred in him stood by him, so that he succeeded in what he desired. How wonderful was the longing that was in him to revive the heart of the people with the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord, with the spirit of the Torah and of enlightenment! As a bright light this is revealed to our eyes when we see that he did new things in the land, such as had not been before him. He made houses for the Torah, to teach the children of Israel knowledge and the Torah of the Lord. In these houses the sons of the prophets grew up, and not many days passed before a band of prophets was already met with, with Samuel standing as head over them [1 Samuel 19:20]. The place in which he founded a faithful house to educate the sons of the prophets according to his way was Ramah, for there was his home. The place of assembly was called Naioth, and this is a name for a house of study of the Torah, for in it the Torah was expounded. This work became a blessing among his people. From these Naioth the Torah went forth, and they were an opened source for a new spirit and for enlightenment. From it springs of wisdom spread forth, and historical literature grew and bore fruit; it was this that was the first foundation of the book of Samuel that we have (1 Chronicles 29:29). And without doubt poetic and prophetic literature also began to flourish then; the pleasant songs and the sublime poems that David sang are surely children of this time. We also have plain traces that Samuel did not cling to the material side of the statutes of the Torah, but for him the main thing was the purpose of the statute and its moral spirit. This is shown to us by the words said in his name concerning the service of the sacrifices. He was the first to speak against the outward act in that service, and he said that the outward act is not the main thing, and the Lord has no delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obeying the voice of the Lord: "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams" (1 Samuel 15). How sublime are these words against the error of the mass of men, who think that the outward act in the performance of the sacrifices suffices to obtain favour from the Lord! But Samuel taught by this that it is not so, and God has no delight except in obeying His voice. For a man who holds these views it will not be hard to think that the Torah too does not insist on the form of some statute. Hence it is not surprising if we find that in his time they sometimes offered a female burnt offering, which is not according to the law of the Torah (1 Samuel 6:14). And he himself offered such a burnt offering (ibid. 7:9). True, the Talmud (Avodah Zarah 24b) wants to find an explanation, and says that Samuel did so on a private high place, and that what the men of Beth-shemesh did was nothing but a ruling for the hour. But where is the permission to depart from the statute of the Torah altogether, even for an hour? And on what did Samuel rely to permit a female burnt offering on a private high place? It can only be that with them the main thing was the purpose of the sacrifice, whatever its form might be. Therefore Samuel departed only from the form of the statute. He thought that although the Torah gave a statute that every burnt offering be of the males, it was not said on that account that a female burnt offering would not be accepted; rather, in truth, if one brought a female burnt offering with a pure intention, it too was acceptable before the Lord. And this ancient opinion left a remnant, in part, also in the later generations, who likewise decided that several matters concerning the form were said only as a commandment, and departing from them does not prevent the acceptance of the sacrifice (Zevaḥim 47a and in many places; and see Pesaḥim 63a and the Tosafot).

1.note: Printed so; no such word; perhaps a misprint for מבצע ('from greed'), which the context suggests.

rows.en: A great thing was brought about in his time, which had great force down to the end of all the generations of the kingdom of Israel: the change in the manner of governing the people and the land. Behold, since the house of Israel was founded to be a nation and a kingdom, it was not destined to stand under the rule of a king. Rather, from the very beginning its kingdom was called a kingdom of priests, with the Lord at their head as their king. The priests, who were set apart to be holy, were not appointed to be rulers but to be ministers, and they were called holy only because they offer the bread of their God (Leviticus 21). And above all, it lay in the will of the divine lawgiver that there be one law for all, the people as the priest, the small as the great, and not that the people be divided into separate groups, as was the case in Egypt and among other peoples besides them. And who knows whether this was not also the cause of the complaint that Korah made — according to what is told in the Torah — against Moses and against Aaron? For Korah and his congregation thought that they wished to raise themselves above the people of the Lord after the manner of the land of Egypt, where the king stands in the place of God on earth and the people serve him with divine worship (Diodorus I, 90), and the priests are holy to God; and they thought that Moses and Aaron too sought to raise themselves to this rank. Now according to this national character it was fitting that there be no royal dominion over them, but that their king be the Lord God. But that the setting up of a king in Israel would be a breach of the statute of the Torah, this is not written explicitly; yet it emerges explicitly from Samuel's refusal. For when they asked for a king, he refused with all the efforts of his strength to give them a king. And why did he refuse so? Because he thought that the setting up of a king was against the statute of the Torah and against the will and intention of the lawgiver. And without doubt the reason for this was like the reason for several statutes that are aimed against idolatry and at striving to keep it far away: so too the divine lawgiver saw that the setting up of a king could bring them to such corrupt opinions, that they would serve their king with divine worship after the manner of the land of Egypt. And Samuel says explicitly in the name of the Lord: "They have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me, that I should not reign over them" (1 Samuel 9:7).⚠1 Now since this is not a statute written and known explicitly from the days of Moses, it must have been a known tradition, living among the people. And have we not seen that already in the days of Gideon, when he prevailed over Midian and all the men of Israel said to him, "Rule over us, both you and your son and your son's son," he answered them and said, "I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you" (Judges 8:22–23)? Already then this idea was known and widespread in the nation. True, Samuel, for all that he refused to set a king over them, nevertheless set aside his opinion, passed over the statute and did as they wished; but this event is certainly a fitting interpretation of the statute in Deuteronomy concerning the king. For there it says: "When you come to the land ... and shall say, I will set a king over me ... you shall surely set him king over you whom the Lord your God shall choose; from among your brethren shall you set a king over you" (Deuteronomy 17). The matter of Samuel proves that this statute is neither a commandment nor a right to set a king over them, but a permission without the will of the Torah (see Sifre, piska 156). However, this time too we are forced to mention here the system of those who deny the unity of the Torah, according to which this statute in Deuteronomy is later than the time of Samuel, or was written in his time and is none other than "the manner of the kingdom" which Samuel "wrote in a book and laid up before the Lord" (1 Samuel 10:25). Now how will our words be believed according to this system, when we say that the matter of Samuel is the interpretation of the statute, seeing that the statute is an outgrowth of the event? To this we say: besides the fact that this is not our position, and that we think this statute is truly ancient, and that "the manner of the kingdom" does not refer to the statute; and we also see no necessity to give such a statute at a time when the kingdom in Israel was already under the hand of a king through human action; and Samuel's refusal is not surprising either, even though there was an explicit statute, "you shall surely set a king over you," because this statute is only a permission not from the will of the Torah — besides all these, surely every intelligent person will in any case agree with us that there is in the words of Samuel and in the words of Gideon the trace of an old tradition. And now, whatever his opinion on the unity of the Torah may be, this will not harm our purpose, and it is enough for us that we have seen that even the deniers agree with us on this. On the contrary: just as they reduce and diminish the written Torah, so they are forced to increase and enlarge the tradition, for every single part of the Torah whose writing they place later was, in their view, surely received in the nation and alive within it.{v1_02_18:1} Therefore in any case it is clear that this principle, that the setting up of a king is against the intention of the Torah, was received in the nation even though it is not written, and it serves to interpret the written statute.

1.note: The verse is 1 Samuel 8:7; the print has ט'.

rows.en: The moral results that came out of Samuel's activity had already grown and prospered in his time, and more after his time. From the day that Saul came to the kingship he strove with all his might to remove from the land every vain and foolish custom and every corrupt belief (1 Samuel 23:3).⚠1 Therefore from the narratives of history too we sometimes perceive how a statute in the Torah was understood. A plain example for this matter comes to us from the story of the war that Saul fought with the Philistines at Michmash. For then, when they prevailed over their enemies, the people flew upon the spoil and slew sheep and oxen on the ground and ate them with the blood. And when they told Saul, "Behold, the people sin against the Lord, in that they eat with the blood," he said: "You have dealt treacherously; roll a great stone to me this day ... and slay them here and eat, and do not sin against the Lord in eating with the blood" (ibid. 14). And Saul's warning in this is without doubt aimed at the statute of the Torah, "You shall not eat with the blood" (Leviticus 19). Now for us today this statute is like a sealed thing, and its matter is hidden from us; but at the time it was given they knew what the sense of this saying was, and what was meant by the expression "eating with the blood." We can only judge, from the fact that this statute comes together with "you shall not use enchantment nor observe times" [Leviticus 19:26], that like them, eating with the blood was a kind of worship among the nations (Ibn Ezra and Ralbag). And if the sages, the bearers of the Oral Torah, handed down to us other and different interpretations of the notion of eating with the blood, this is only because already in their time eating with the blood was no longer among the rites of idolatry, as it had been in ancient days. But in truth the intent of the statute, first and foremost, was nothing other than what we said: that it was a custom of the nations to eat the flesh of the slaughtered animal in the place where its blood was poured out, and they sat around the blood, and this was their manner of worship to their idols. Now if we consider the story mentioned, this true interpretation emerges for us. For on what does Saul place the main weight of his complaint against the people? Only on their slaughtering on the ground and eating with the blood. Therefore what was evil in his eyes and counted as a sin was nothing other than that they slaughtered on the earth, and the blood was on the earth, and there they ate the flesh beside the blood poured out on the ground. And against this practice he commanded them to slaughter upon the great stone that they rolled to him, and then they could eat in any place, but at a distance from the blood, and they would not sin against the statute in the Torah. This custom persisted for many more days, that they were wont to eat with the blood as a form of worship of idols, and even in the days of the prophet Ezekiel we find a trace of it (Ezekiel 33:25), where he tells his people their transgressions, and one particular among them is that they ate with the blood and lifted up their eyes to their idols.{v1_02_19:1}

1.note: Saul's removal of the mediums and wizards is 1 Samuel 28:3; the print has כ"ג.

footnotes.en: See the *History of the People of Israel* by Eisenlohr, vol. 2, pp. 42, 29, and what he quotes there from the book on the Canaanites by Movers, vol. 2, p. 318.

See Bavli Sanhedrin (39a)⚠1 and Ta'anit (4a), what is said there on the verse (2 Kings 3:27) "Then he took his son ... and offered him for a burnt offering; and there was great wrath against Israel." But the plain sense of the verse is certainly that he offered him to the Lord God of Israel.

1.note: The passage on Mesha's son is at Sanhedrin 39b; the print has ל"ט. (39a).

footnotes.en: In the Gemara, Bava Batra (14b), the scroll of Ruth is ascribed to the prophet Samuel. Without doubt they were moved to hold this opinion by seeing that the whole purpose of the book was to trace the lineage of David to the tribe of Judah, which was destined to be the one from which the rulers in Israel would come forth; and since Samuel sought to found the kingship in the house of David, he saw fit to set forth his lineage first, to show that the kingship befits him by his descent. But to this argument there is an answer. First, we do not find that it was made public in Samuel's lifetime that he had anointed David king; for he did all this in secret. A second thing is proved from the phrase "And it came to pass in the days when the judges judged" [Ruth 1:1]: that between the writer and the Judges a long time lies. It is more fitting to ascribe the composition of this scroll to the time of the division of the kingdom, that is, the time of Rehoboam, when the author wished to show the lineage of the house of David. Yet this too is forced, for then there would be only five generations between the time of the writer and the time of the event; and from his saying there, "Now this was the custom in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning exchanging" [Ruth 4:7], it appears that there was a great distance between the time of the writer and the time of the event. This too is a proof against the view of the Gemara that Samuel wrote it. Some place it as late as the time of the exile (see the commentary of the Christian scholar Bertheau on Judges and Ruth, p. 237), and his proofs are from the character of the language, in which Aramaic traces are already found, such as timtse'in, tidbakin, teda'in, ta'asin, kayyem, Mara; and Shaddai is found in place of El Shaddai, and the whole phrase has a parallel in the book of Job: "and Shaddai has dealt very bitterly with me." We also find that this composition has a reflective character: it is not enough for it to tell only the events that happened before it,⚠1 but it adds to them also its reflection on them, as when it explains the ancient custom and its difference from the custom of its own time concerning the manner of acquisition. Of this kind too is what it adds at the end of the composition, the lineage of David; and this custom was not found among the writers of chronicles of ancient times. But for all this we have a clear proof that the scroll was written at an early time, from what is said there: "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance." By the word "his inheritance" the speaker without doubt intended the purpose of the statute under discussion, which is that an inheritance not pass from tribe to tribe; and certainly at the time of its writing they still guarded the permanence of the inheritance according to the division of the land among the tribes. And it is a wonder that in Deuteronomy nothing is mentioned of raising up the name of the dead upon the inheritance.

1.note: Print blurred at this point; read שארעו לנגד[ו], 'that happened before it'.

footnotes.en: See Yerushalmi Kiddushin 1:1 and Midrash Ruth: "At first they used to acquire by drawing off the shoe; they changed to acquire by kezatsah; they changed to acquire by money, by deed and by possession." It is explicit that this mode of acquisition ceased at some time, and then it returned to its old form, to acquire by a kerchief, which is like drawing off the shoe (Bava Metzi'a 47a). And it had already become unknown how this acquisition worked — who gave to whom? (Yerushalmi, and Bavli ibid.). This is a sign that the custom had lapsed for a long time.

I have seen fit to remark here on the view of the one who says (Makkot 11a) that Joshua wrote the section of the cities of refuge in the Torah, which the Gemara strained to explain. According to our way we say that his intention is that this commandment was among the things that Joshua received from Moses orally, and when the time came to fulfil it, that is, after the conquest and the settlement, he wrote them in the Torah; and he learned this from the language of the verse in Joshua 20:2: "Speak to the children of Israel, saying: Appoint for yourselves the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you by the hand of Moses"; from his saying "of which I spoke" he understood that the speech was oral. And if this is his intention, we learn that Joshua was the first who wrote down oral matters.
